questions.stem: Change to passive voice: 'The teacher punished the student.'

options.option_text: The student was punishing the teacher.
The student was punished by the teacher.
The teacher was punished by the student.
The student has been punished by the teacher.

questions.explanation: B is correct. Active: 'The teacher punished the student.' Subject=teacher, verb=punished (past), object=student. Passive: Object becomes subject → 'The student'; past passive = 'was punished'; by + original subject = 'by the teacher'. → 'The student was punished by the teacher.'

questions.stem: Change to active voice: 'The letter was written by Priya.'

options.option_text: Priya is writing the letter.
Priya wrote the letter.
The letter wrote by Priya.
Priya has written the letter.

questions.explanation: B is correct. Passive: 'The letter was written by Priya.' → Active: Agent (Priya) becomes subject; verb 'was written' (past passive) → 'wrote' (simple past); 'the letter' becomes object. → 'Priya wrote the letter.'

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly converts 'She is baking a cake.' to passive voice?

options.option_text: A cake is baked by her.
A cake is being baked by her.
A cake was being baked by her.
A cake has been baked by her.

questions.explanation: B is correct. Active (present continuous): 'She is baking a cake.' Passive formula for present continuous: Object + is/am/are + being + V3 + by + Subject. → 'A cake is being baked by her.' Key pattern: is baking → is being baked.

questions.stem: Change to passive voice: 'They have completed the project.'

options.option_text: The project was completed by them.
The project has been completed by them.
The project is completed by them.
The project had been completed by them.

questions.explanation: B is correct. Active (present perfect): 'They have completed the project.' Passive formula: Object + has/have + been + V3 + by + Subject. → 'The project has been completed by them.' Key: have completed → has been completed (subject is singular 'project' → has).

questions.stem: Change to passive: 'Who broke the window?'

options.option_text: By whom the window was broken?
By whom was the window broken?
The window was broken by whom?
By who was the window broken?

questions.explanation: B is correct. Active question: 'Who broke the window?' For interrogative passive: 'By whom' + was/were + object + V3. → 'By whom was the window broken?' Note: 'whom' not 'who' — it is the object of the preposition 'by'. The question format requires inversion (was before 'the window').

questions.stem: Which sentence is in passive voice?

options.option_text: The dog bit the postman.
The manager called the meeting.
The new policy was announced by the minister.
She reads novels every evening.

questions.explanation: C is correct. Passive voice: the subject receives the action; verb form = auxiliary (was/is/has been etc.) + past participle (V3); often followed by 'by + agent'. 'The new policy WAS ANNOUNCED by the minister' — 'the new policy' does not announce; the minister does. This is passive voice.

questions.stem: Change to passive voice: 'They will announce the results tomorrow.'

options.option_text: The results will be announced tomorrow by them.
The results would be announced by them tomorrow.
The results are to be announced by them.
The results were announced by them tomorrow.

questions.explanation: A is correct. Active (simple future): 'They will announce the results tomorrow.' Passive formula: Object + will + be + V3 + by + Subject. → 'The results will be announced by them tomorrow.' Note: 'tomorrow' stays in its natural position at the end.

questions.stem: Change to active voice: 'Let the door be closed.'

options.option_text: Close the door.
Someone is closing the door.
The door has been closed.
You should close the door.

questions.explanation: A is correct. Passive imperative: 'Let the door be closed.' Active imperative conversion: remove 'Let' and 'be', convert past participle back to base form, make it a direct command. → 'Close the door.' This is the standard rule for converting passive imperatives to active imperatives.

questions.stem: Identify the voice in: 'The cake tastes delicious.'

options.option_text: Passive
Active
Both active and passive
Neither

questions.explanation: B is correct. This is ACTIVE voice — a common trap. 'The cake tastes delicious' uses a STATIVE verb (tastes, smells, looks, feels, sounds). Although 'the cake' doesn't actively do anything, there is no passive structure (no auxiliary + past participle). Stative verbs like taste, smell, look, feel, sound are active in structure. Passive would be: 'The cake is tasted by someone' — different meaning entirely.

questions.stem: Change to passive: 'Nobody has informed me of the changes.'

options.option_text: The changes have not been informed to me.
I have not been informed of the changes.
I was not informed of the changes.
Me has not been informed of the changes.

questions.explanation: B is correct. Active: 'Nobody has informed me of the changes.' When the agent is 'nobody', it is dropped in passive. 'Me' (indirect object) becomes subject 'I'. 'has informed' → 'have been informed' (present perfect passive). → 'I have not been informed of the changes.' Note: negative preserved by 'not'.
